svg.title: From a chemical compound to a verified filter for a safety rule
svg.desc: Four stages from left to right. A chemical compound, which can come from the real world or from a deep generative chemistry model: here (2R,3E)-pent-3-en-2-ol, shown as a ball-and-stick model. Its machine-readable formats in cheminformatics: a molecular graph, the SMILES text C/C=C/[C@@H](C)O, an InChI, and others. The Lean 4 Mol object that VeriMol reads from the SMILES text: six atoms, five bonds and two stereo facts. And a verified safety filter, made by vericoding. At the top, a filter for a safety rule, between an AI that proposes molecules and the lab: a chemist states the rule, an AI writes the checker and its proof, and Lean checks the proof. The rule that is built: no long perfluorinated group. It is shown on the formula of PFOA (perfluorooctanoic acid), which has a group of seven carbon atoms that carry fluorine. Compounds with perfluorinated groups are PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances), called forever chemicals because they hardly break down; PFOA is a long-chain PFAS. A proposal is asked three questions, whether it is read, whether the Mol is sound and whether the rule holds, and only then is it handed on to the lab. The theorem of the filter says that it hands on a Mol exactly when the text is read as that Mol, the Mol is sound, and the rule holds. With the number 6, ibuprofen is handed on and PFOA is refused for a group of 7. Under it, the foundation, proven about the reader and the writer: reading gives a well-formed graph, reading inverts writing, and a canonical text names one molecule. More kinds of rules are marked as outlook.
svg.text: PFOA, a long-chain PFAS: a group of 7
Compounds with perfluorinated groups are PFAS,
the “forever chemicals”: they hardly break down.
a canonical text names one molecule
the atoms, numbered in the order of the SMILES text
every proof checked by Lean’s kernel
